theory.intro: Some trigonometric equations are quadratics in disguise. Move every term to one side, use a Pythagorean identity if two different ratios appear, then factorise and solve each factor on the given domain.
facts: A quadratic in a ratio, such as $2\sin^2\theta - \sin\theta - 1 = 0$, factorises just like $2u^2 - u - 1 = 0$ with $u = \sin\theta$.
If two different ratios appear, use $\sin^2\theta = 1 - \cos^2\theta$, $\cos^2\theta = 1 - \sin^2\theta$ or $\sec^2\theta = 1 + \tan^2\theta$ to get a single ratio.
**Never divide** both sides by a trigonometric term, because that throws away every solution where the term is zero.
Reject any factor giving $|\sin\theta| > 1$ or $|\cos\theta| > 1$, since no angle has such a ratio.
Taking the square root of $\operatorname{trig}^2\theta = k$ gives both signs, $\operatorname{trig}\theta = \pm\sqrt{k}$, so solutions appear in all four quadrants.
steps: Rearrange to standard form and substitute Pythagorean identities if needed
Apply the null factor law and reject impossible roots
Solve each valid linear equation on the domain

foundation.solution_text:
$4\sin^2\theta - 3 = 0$
$4\sin^2\theta = 3$
$\sin^2\theta = \dfrac{3}{4}$
$\sin\theta = \pm\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$
Reference angle: $\theta_{\text{ref}} = 60^{\circ}$
Solutions lie in all four quadrants:
Quadrant 1: $\theta = 60^{\circ}$
Quadrant 2: $\theta = 180^{\circ} - 60^{\circ} = 120^{\circ}$
Quadrant 3: $\theta = 180^{\circ} + 60^{\circ} = 240^{\circ}$
Quadrant 4: $\theta = 360^{\circ} - 60^{\circ} = 300^{\circ}$
$\theta = 60^{\circ}, 120^{\circ}, 240^{\circ}, 300^{\circ}$

$2\sin^2 x - 3\sin x + 1 = 0$
$(2\sin x - 1)(\sin x - 1) = 0$
$\sin x = \dfrac{1}{2}$ or $\sin x = 1$
When $\sin x = \dfrac{1}{2}$:
$x = \dfrac{\pi}{6}, \dfrac{5\pi}{6}$
When $\sin x = 1$:
$x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$
$x = \dfrac{\pi}{6}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{5\pi}{6}$

$2\cos^2 x - \cos x - 1 = 0$
$(2\cos x + 1)(\cos x - 1) = 0$
$\cos x = -\dfrac{1}{2}$ or $\cos x = 1$
When $\cos x = -\dfrac{1}{2}$:
$x = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}, \dfrac{4\pi}{3}$
When $\cos x = 1$:
$x = 0$
$x = 0, \dfrac{2\pi}{3}, \dfrac{4\pi}{3}$

$2\sin^2\theta + 3\sin\theta - 2 = 0$
$(2\sin\theta - 1)(\sin\theta + 2) = 0$
$\sin\theta = \dfrac{1}{2}$ or $\sin\theta = -2$
Since $-1 \le \sin\theta \le 1$, $\sin\theta = -2$ has no real solutions.
When $\sin\theta = \dfrac{1}{2}$:
$\theta = 30^{\circ}, 150^{\circ}$
$\theta = 30^{\circ}, 150^{\circ}$

development.solution_text:
$2\cos^2\theta - 1 = 0$
$2\cos^2\theta = 1$
$\cos^2\theta = \dfrac{1}{2}$
$\cos\theta = \pm\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$
Reference angle: $\theta_{\text{ref}} = 45^{\circ}$
Solutions in all four quadrants:
Quadrant 1: $\theta = 45^{\circ}$
Quadrant 2: $\theta = 180^{\circ} - 45^{\circ} = 135^{\circ}$
Quadrant 3: $\theta = 180^{\circ} + 45^{\circ} = 225^{\circ}$
Quadrant 4: $\theta = 360^{\circ} - 45^{\circ} = 315^{\circ}$
$\theta = 45^{\circ}, 135^{\circ}, 225^{\circ}, 315^{\circ}$

$2\sin^2 x + \cos x - 2 = 0$
$2(1 - \cos^2 x) + \cos x - 2 = 0$
$2 - 2\cos^2 x + \cos x - 2 = 0$
$-2\cos^2 x + \cos x = 0$
$\cos x(1 - 2\cos x) = 0$
$\cos x = 0$ or $\cos x = \dfrac{1}{2}$
When $\cos x = 0$:
$x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{3\pi}{2}$
When $\cos x = \dfrac{1}{2}$:
$x = \dfrac{\pi}{3}, \dfrac{5\pi}{3}$
$x = \dfrac{\pi}{3}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{3\pi}{2}, \dfrac{5\pi}{3}$

$2\cos^2\theta - 5\cos\theta + 2 = 0$
$(2\cos\theta - 1)(\cos\theta - 2) = 0$
$\cos\theta = \dfrac{1}{2}$ or $\cos\theta = 2$
Since $-1 \le \cos\theta \le 1$, $\cos\theta = 2$ has no real solutions.
When $\cos\theta = \dfrac{1}{2}$:
$\theta = 60^{\circ}, 300^{\circ}$
$\theta = 60^{\circ}, 300^{\circ}$

$\tan^2 x + \sec x - 1 = 0$
$(\sec^2 x - 1) + \sec x - 1 = 0$
$\sec^2 x + \sec x - 2 = 0$
$(\sec x + 2)(\sec x - 1) = 0$
$\sec x = 1$ or $\sec x = -2$
When $\sec x = 1$:
$\cos x = 1 \implies x = 0$
When $\sec x = -2$:
$\cos x = -\dfrac{1}{2} \implies x = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}, \dfrac{4\pi}{3}$
$x = 0, \dfrac{2\pi}{3}, \dfrac{4\pi}{3}$

$\cos x = \sec x$
$\cos x = \dfrac{1}{\cos x}$
$\cos^2 x = 1$
$\cos x = \pm 1$
When $\cos x = 1$:
$x = 0$
When $\cos x = -1$:
$x = \pi$
$x = 0, \pi$

mastery.question_text: Solve $\cos^2 x - \sin^2 x = 3\sin x - 1$ for $-\pi \le x \le \pi$.
mastery.solution_text:
$\cos^2 x - \sin^2 x = 3\sin x - 1$
$(1 - \sin^2 x) - \sin^2 x = 3\sin x - 1$
$1 - 2\sin^2 x = 3\sin x - 1$
$2\sin^2 x + 3\sin x - 2 = 0$
$(2\sin x - 1)(\sin x + 2) = 0$
$\sin x = \dfrac{1}{2}$ or $\sin x = -2$
Since $-1 \le \sin x \le 1$, $\sin x = -2$ has no real solutions.
When $\sin x = \dfrac{1}{2}$ for $-\pi \le x \le \pi$:
$x = \dfrac{\pi}{6}, \dfrac{5\pi}{6}$
$x = \dfrac{\pi}{6}, \dfrac{5\pi}{6}$
